cards.back: 81 mg. "You never give babies aspirin"

cards.front: Why does aspirin raise the risk of GI bleeding?
cards.back: Increased bleeding risk plus gastric irritation

cards.front: Aspirin in children and adolescents
cards.back: "Always avoid." Slide reason: Reye syndrome risk with viral illnesses

cards.front: The one P2Y12 difference that matters: what's true of clopidogrel (Plavix)?
cards.back: More possible drug interactions, because of CYP450

cards.front: Why does DAPT combine aspirin with a P2Y12 inhibitor?
cards.back: It suppresses two separate pathways (COX-1 → TXA₂ and ADP), so platelet suppression is greater

cards.front: DAPT stopped too soon and the new stent clots off: result?
cards.back: "It's a giant MI"

cards.front: Can a client stop DAPT on their own?
cards.back: No: only when the prescriber knows and agrees

cards.front: Eptifibatide (Integrilin) and tirofiban (Aggrastat): what do they block?
cards.back: GP IIb/IIIa: the bridge between platelets, the final step of aggregation

cards.front: When are GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors given?
cards.back: IV, only during a stenting or other high-risk cardiovascular procedure; not on a floor every 12 hours

cards.front: What is alteplase (Activase)?
cards.back: Recombinant tPA, made in a lab; far more than the body would ever produce at once

cards.front: Alteplase (Activase): the three major indications
cards.back: Acute ischemic stroke · high-risk pulmonary embolism · STEMI (not unstable angina or NSTEMI) when timely PCI is unavailable

cards.front: Stroke symptoms: first test before any thrombolytic?
cards.back: Head CT, to rule out hemorrhagic stroke. Chest pain → EKG first; stroke symptoms → head CT first

cards.front: Alteplase (Activase) vs anticoagulants: effect on an existing clot
cards.back: Anticoagulants don't directly dissolve it; alteplase promotes degradation of fibrin already present

cards.front: Most serious complication of thrombolytics
cards.back: Intracranial hemorrhage

cards.front: STEMI client with horrible injuries from a car crash: give the thrombolytic?
cards.back: No: "Can't give the thrombolytic, right?" Active bleeding is a contraindication

cards.front: Major contraindications to thrombolytics
cards.back: Active significant bleeding · known or suspected intracranial hemorrhage · certain recent intracranial injuries or procedures · severe uncontrolled hypertension

cards.front: Tachycardia: effect on time in diastole, and why do we care?
cards.back: Decreases it. "The perfusion through the vessels of the heart" happens during diastole

cards.front: Principal antianginal benefit of sublingual nitroglycerin?
cards.back: "This big reduction in preload, which is going to decrease cardiac workload overall"

cards.front: Pain at rest, ischemic EKG changes, no persistent ST elevation, troponin below threshold: diagnosis?
cards.back: "Good, so it's unstable angina"

cards.front: AF with a ventricular rate of 132: the two problems to treat
cards.back: "Rapid ventricular response, so we need to get that rate under control" and stasis of blood leading to thrombus, so "we need to anticoagulate"

cards.front: Potassium effects: thiazides and loops vs ACE inhibitors and ARBs
cards.back: "Thiazides and loops are gonna be hypokalemia"; ACE inhibitors and ARBs, hyperkalemia

cards.front: HFrEF: the four pillars
cards.back: "Something for RAS, a beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist" and "the SGLT2 inhibitors"

qa.q: (student asked) Would heparin and Lovenox be given at the same time?
qa.a: No. They're similar in structure, but "we wouldn't give them at the same time" because Lovenox is a low-molecular-weight heparin. She then used the question as a segue into comparing them.

qa.q: (student asked) Can Lovenox be used for heparin bridging?
qa.a: "No, because we need the drip." Bridging needs the heparin drip because the clotting risk is high; the person is often hospitalized for that part.

qa.q: (student asked) Why use warfarin rather than heparin for atrial fibrillation?
qa.a: Route first: heparins are injections, warfarin is oral. It's also much harder to reach the needed degree of anticoagulation with heparin injections; "warfarin just does a really good job" preventing clots in the atria.

qa.q: (student asked) Does a higher INR mean more bleeding?
qa.a: Yes: more risk of bleeding. About 1 when not anticoagulated; 2 to 3 is the range.

qa.q: (student asked; question not fully audible) Why give vitamin K along with 4F-PCC when reversing warfarin?
qa.a: 4F-PCC replaces the factors for now, but those only last a little while. Vitamin K helps the liver build its own over the next several days. It depends whether reversal needs to last several days or only a little while.

qa.q: (student asked) How does a nurse handle DOAC timing when a patient travels across time zones?
qa.a: Start by talking through how it will affect their life. A smartphone alarm is the biggest tool now. Shift workers or heavy travelers who can't keep the schedule may be better served by warfarin.

qa.q: (student asked) What about DIC?
qa.a: Not this lecture. "We will get to DIC" when shock is covered.

qa.q: (student asked) Does a DOAC have to be taken at the same time each dose?
qa.a: As close as possible, within about a half hour before or after the chosen time. After a missed dose, get the next dose on board as soon as possible; each drug comes with specific missed-dose instructions.

qa.q: (student asked) Can patients monitor their INR at home, like blood sugar?
qa.a: Home setups exist but are expensive and harder than a glucose stick. Dosing depends so heavily on the number that "the home ones have not gotten to the point yet where we're feeling consistently good about them."

qa.q: (student asked) Why use a DOAC rather than heparin or enoxaparin for atrial fibrillation?
qa.a: UFH and enoxaparin aren't strong enough for AFib, except a heparin drip bridging to warfarin. They're "kind of weaker, which is nice for prophylaxis"; the stronger drugs are for patients who need them.

qa.q: (student asked) Why does a mechanical valve need warfarin rather than a DOAC?
qa.a: "It's strength." A mechanical valve goes click, click, click, causes turbulence and is a very high clot risk; warfarin is the only drug that gets anticoagulation as high as needed.

qa.q: If I call EMS and say I'm having chest pain and I think I'm having a heart attack, what do they tell people first?
qa.a: A student offered nitroglycerin: "if they have nitroglycerin, absolutely." But if there's aspirin in the house, take one and chew it, not just swallow it, so it is absorbed as quickly as possible.

qa.q: (student asked) How long does a patient stay on DAPT after a stent?
qa.a: A variable amount of time, depending on the stent type (drug-eluting vs bare metal), with specific time frames; more in adult health. Some high-risk patients simply stay on it. If the stent clots off, "it's a giant MI."

qa.q: A patient has a STEMI, crashes the car because of it, and now has horrible injuries. "Can't give the thrombolytic, right?"
qa.a: Right. "If they're already bleeding, we're not going to give it." Active bleeding is a contraindication.

qa.q: (student asked) What is reperfusion injury?
qa.a: Returning blood to tissue deprived of oxygen brings free radicals, inflammatory mediators and clotting factors into play. Still "way better than not reperfusing at all." More with stroke.

qa.q: If we have increased systemic vascular resistance, what effect does that have on afterload?
qa.a: Class: increases. More constriction means higher afterload.

qa.q: How does that higher afterload affect left ventricular workload and oxygen demand?
qa.a: Class: both increase.

qa.q: If we have lower venous return, what happens to preload?
qa.a: Class: decreases. Less preload.

qa.q: If we have tachycardia, what is the effect on oxygen demand?
qa.a: Class: increases.

qa.q: What is the effect of tachycardia on time in diastole, and why do we care?
qa.a: Class: decreases. Coronary perfusion happens during diastole, so too little diastole can decrease flow; a slower heart gets more time and improved flow.

qa.q: A 61-year-old with hypertension, elevated LDL and tobacco exposure has had chest pressure on stairs that resolves with rest. What about the original pattern was stable?
qa.a: It came on predictably with increased cardiac workload and predictably went away with rest: a fixed plaque limiting flow.

qa.q: Today that patient had chest pressure at rest lasting 25 minutes. What process could account for the new symptoms?
qa.a: Class: something is going on with the plaque. It's at least starting to erode, with some platelet aggregation, large or small. That's why it's called acute coronary syndrome.

qa.q: (student asked) What is the difference between plaque erosion and rupture?
qa.a: Rupture is like pulling off the whole scab. Erosion is like rubbing against it: the collagen cap slowly breaks down until a little underlying tissue is exposed. Platelets start to bind, a small warning rather than a huge rupture.

qa.q: What distinguishes ischemia from necrosis? Can we reverse ischemia?
qa.a: Ischemia is reduced blood supply and is potentially reversible, without large troponin levels. Infarction is cells dying and releasing their contents, including troponin.

qa.q: Which change explains the principal antianginal benefit of sublingual nitroglycerin?
qa.a: Class answered correctly ("very good"): the big reduction in preload, which decreases cardiac workload overall.

qa.q: A patient has pain at rest, ischemic EKG changes without persistent ST elevation, and serial troponin that stays below the injury threshold. Which would the patient have?
qa.a: Class: unstable angina ("Good"). Troponin above threshold would make it an NSTEMI; ST elevation would make it a STEMI.

qa.q: (student asked) Will the exam include rhythm strips?
qa.a: No strips. "I have one question that verbally describes a rhythm"; if you saw this, what would you most likely do?

qa.q: A 73-year-old with chronic hypertension has atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 132. We want the rate down. What is the other type of medication we need?
qa.a: Class: anticoagulation ("Good"). Problem one is rapid ventricular response, needing rate control. Problem two is stasis of blood leading to thrombus formation.

qa.q: What is a thiazide doing?
qa.a: Class: diuretic ("excellent"). It reduces sodium reabsorption, so less water is reabsorbed.

qa.q: Besides low blood pressure, what are the other adverse effects of thiazides? Which electrolyte is the biggest?
qa.a: Class: electrolytes, with potassium the biggest. Hypokalemia, not quite as much as loops.

qa.q: What are the major side effects of ACE inhibitors and ARBs?
qa.a: Class: cough. The more severe bradykinin effect is angioedema; also hyperkalemia. "Thiazides and loops are hypokalemia; ACE inhibitors and ARBs, hyperkalemia."

qa.q: Beta blockers: what are they going to do?
qa.a: Decrease heart rate and contractility, which decreases cardiac output, half of the blood-pressure equation. Check heart rate first; they can mask hypoglycemia symptoms in diabetes.

qa.q: How do dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers work in general, and what is their odd side effect?
qa.a: Class: vascular ("Good"). Arterial vasodilation lowers systemic vascular resistance. Peripheral edema is common: some swelling in the ankles and feet, not giant pitting edema.

qa.q: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers: what area do they like?
qa.a: Class: heart rate. Decreased rate and contractility lower cardiac output, with bradycardia as the side effect, but they don't mask hypoglycemia.

qa.q: A 67-year-old with a prior MI, EF 30%, orthopnea, crackles, JVD and ankle edema. Why does low cardiac output trigger fluid retention?
qa.a: Class answered ("Yep"): it's sensed by the kidneys, with renin release. Baroreceptors also notice and activate the SNS.

qa.q: On furosemide, losartan, metoprolol and spironolactone: which reduce symptoms only, and which address the underlying cause?
qa.a: Furosemide is symptoms only. Losartan, metoprolol and spironolactone block the angiotensin, SNS and aldosterone drive behind remodeling.

qa.q: That patient has HFrEF and we want four pillars. Which drug is missing? The class originally created for diabetes.
qa.a: Class: SGLT2 inhibitors. The four: a RAS drug, a beta blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor.

qa.q: What electrolyte changes would you anticipate on that regimen?
qa.a: Potassium: losartan and spironolactone raise it, furosemide lowers it. Watch it closely and adjust; the drugs are too important to stop for that.
